topic: Application pipeline: apply in waves, run three or four loops in parallel
why: An FDE job search is structurally identical to the job itself: a portfolio of accounts at different stages, each with a different stakeholder, each moving at a speed you do not control, all needing to be sequenced so decisions land when you need them to. Run serially, a search produces one decision every eight weeks and zero leverage; run as an instrumented pipeline with three or four loops converging, it produces two offers in the same fortnight and a real choice. The same instincts a hiring manager is testing - do you keep every thread alive with an owner and a due date, do you force a decision instead of waiting, do you tell the truth when timelines collide - are exactly the ones this topic drills, which is why running your own pipeline badly is itself a signal.
prerequisites: Three public case studies live with a single index link you can paste into any application (topic 80) - the pipeline moves at the speed of your artifacts, and you cannot tailor what does not exist.

The Hermes write-up published and a LinkedIn profile that reads as FDE rather than generic backend (topic 81), because inbound recruiter flow is a channel you will measure and it only exists if the profile does.
A 40-company target list with tiering, named referral paths and warm-intro routes already researched (topic 82). This topic consumes that list; it does not build it.

Enough technical readiness to survive a first-round screen in your two strongest areas today. Requisition cooldowns are 6-12 months at most large companies, so a wave sent before you can pass a screen spends a company you cannot get back.
Working comfort with a spreadsheet or a checked-in CSV as a system of record: formulas or a 60-line script, conditional formatting or a diff, and a scheduled job that emails you a digest.
An interview-ready environment and calendar hygiene - a quiet room, tested screen share and audio, and a calendar where your own blocks are real events rather than intentions.

subtopics.name: Model the search as a pipeline with explicit states and WIP limits
subtopics.learn: Draw the state machine before you open a spreadsheet: sourced, applied, recruiter screen, hiring-manager screen, technical round(s), full loop, team match, offer, decision - plus the terminal states reject, withdrew, ghosted and paused. Every state gets an owner (me or them), an expected dwell time, and a next-action-by date; a company with no next action is not in your pipeline, it is a memory. Set the work-in-progress limit deliberately: 3-4 companies in loop stages (technical onward) at once, because past four your prep time per loop drops below what actually wins rounds, plus 10-14 in the earlier feeding stages. WIP is the control variable you tune every Friday, not something that happens to you.

resource.label: Atlassian Agile Coach - Kanban (boards, work-in-progress limits, flow)

subtopics.name: Funnel math: the six conversion ratios and your own baselines
subtopics.learn: Instrument six ratios and compute each per channel and per wave: application to recruiter response, response to HM screen, screen to technical, technical to full loop, loop to offer, offer to accept. Know the shape of realistic numbers so you can tell a bad process from bad luck - a strong senior profile applying cold sees roughly 5-15% response, a warm referral pushes that first number to 40-60% and moves the loop-to-offer number almost not at all, which is precisely why referrals matter and precisely why they are not a substitute for readiness. Then back-solve: two offers inside one two-week window implies roughly 6-10 loops, which implies 25-40 real applications with a referral mix, not 200 portal submissions. Write the baseline down before wave one so wave two is a comparison rather than a feeling.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Service Level Objectives (choosing indicators and targets)

subtopics.name: Wave sizing with Little's Law: how many applications must be in flight
subtopics.learn: L equals lambda times W. Cycle time W from application to decision is 4-8 weeks at most companies and 8-12 at Palantir-class loops with team matching and a hiring committee. If you want L equals 4 concurrent loops and W is 6 weeks, loops must start at 4/6, about 0.67 per week; at a 25% application-to-loop conversion that is roughly 2.7 applications per week sustained - about 11-12 per two-week wave, forever, not once. Do this arithmetic explicitly, because the non-obvious consequence is that the pipeline you can negotiate with in week 10 was determined by what you sent in week 2. You cannot fix a thin pipeline in the week an offer lands, and every week you skip a wave shows up as an empty slot forty days later.

resource.label: Little's Law (queueing relation between WIP, throughput and cycle time)

subtopics.name: Tracker schema: fields, states, and the one-row-per-application invariant
subtopics.learn: Design the schema once, with the fields that make the weekly review mechanical: company, req_url, req_id, tier, wave, channel (referral, recruiter_inbound, hm_direct, portal), referrer_name, date_applied, stage, stage_entered_at, next_action, next_action_due, owner (me or them), last_contact_at, recruiter_name, recruiter_email, interviewers, artifact_sent, level_target, comp_band_published, comp_anchor_given (boolean), expected_decision_date, outcome, reject_stage, reject_reason_code, notes_url. Enforce three invariants: one row per application, never one per company; stage_entered_at is rewritten on every transition so dwell time per stage is computable at the end; and any row where owner is me and next_action_due is in the past is a defect, not a to-do. Add reject_reason_code as a controlled vocabulary now (prep_gap, communication, scope_mismatch, level_mismatch, headcount_frozen, unknown) - free-text reasons are unanalysable in week ten.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Planning and tracking with Projects (custom fields, views, automation)

subtopics.name: Build it and automate the digest so you never have to check the tracker
subtopics.learn: Whatever the substrate, the rule is that the tracker pushes to you. In Sheets: conditional formatting turning next_action_due red when it is less than TODAY(), a stage histogram and the six ratios computed with COUNTIFS or a single QUERY, a weekly snapshot tab appended by a time-driven Apps Script trigger so you can chart stage counts over time, and a daily 08:00 MailApp.sendEmail digest listing overdue actions plus every row where owner is them and last_contact_at is more than seven days old. If you prefer git: a CSV in the repo, a 60-line Python script producing the same digest, and a cron or GitHub Action running it. Build it in one sitting and then stop building it - a tracker you are still improving in week six is a procrastination artifact.

resource.label: Google Apps Script - Extending Google Sheets (triggers, custom functions)

subtopics.name: Tier the 40 companies and assign waves so wave one is calibration
subtopics.learn: Split the target list from topic 82 into A (you would sign inside 48 hours), B (strong, right level and comp required) and C (fine, mainly loop practice and a floor offer). Then invert the instinct everyone has: wave one is roughly 60% C, 30% B, 10% A. Three reasons, all mechanical - your first three loops are objectively your worst, rejections carry a 6-12 month requisition cooldown at most large companies, and a live C-tier offer is the cheapest negotiating leverage that exists. For every row record the target level and the published or market band for that level and location so tier is a decision you can defend, not a vibe; a company whose band tops out below your floor belongs in C or off the list entirely.

resource.label: Levels.fyi - Software Engineer compensation in the United States (bands by level, company and location)

subtopics.name: Channel strategy and the reality of what a recruiter actually sees
subtopics.learn: Rank the channels by conversion and use them in order: internal referral, warm recruiter or inbound, direct hiring-manager contact, cold portal. Understand what the portal really is - your application lands in an ATS list view where a recruiter sees your name, current title, sometimes one screening-question answer, and decides in seconds; the top third of page one of the resume and the screening answers are therefore the entire product. Two sequencing rules that people get backwards: get the referral in flight before or with the portal submission, because a referral attached to an application that is already sitting in the pile is materially weaker than a referral-sourced application; and apply inside 72 hours of a requisition going live, since review is roughly first-in-first-seen and pipelines close early. Never hold two open applications at one company simultaneously - it reads as spraying.

resource.label: Greenhouse Support - Application review stage (what the recruiter sees per application, the referral priority queue, advance or reject)

subtopics.name: Referral engineering: the forwardable blurb and the ask that converts
subtopics.learn: Write a five-to-six-line blurb in the third person that your contact can paste into Slack with zero editing: who you are, the one number that proves the claim, the specific requisition link, and one sentence on why this company. Make the ask binary and cheap - 'would you be comfortable forwarding this to whoever owns the FDE req? Completely fine if not' - because the open-ended 'can you refer me' silently asks them to write the blurb, which is why it fails. For second-degree paths ask for an introduction to a named person, never a general introduction. Then run the follow-through that determines whether wave three still has referrals available: report back within five business days regardless of outcome, and cap yourself at two asks per contact per quarter. Log referrer_name on the row so the thank-you is scheduled, not remembered.

resource.label: Fred Wilson (AVC) - The Double Opt-In Introduction (the forwardable ask and introductions to a named person)

subtopics.name: Sourcing live requisitions beyond LinkedIn, and the seven title variants
subtopics.learn: LinkedIn misses a large fraction of FDE-shaped roles, and the title is not stable. Every wave, search all of: Forward Deployed Engineer, Forward Deployed Software Engineer, Solutions Engineer, Field Engineer, Deployment Strategist, Applied AI Engineer, and Technical Account Manager where the requisition is genuinely technical. Source from the monthly Hacker News Who Is Hiring thread, YC's startup job board, and company career pages directly - many boards expose a public JSON endpoint you can diff weekly with a short script so new requisitions surface the day they post rather than the week you happen to look. Freshness beats volume: a two-day-old requisition converts several times better than the same one at three weeks.

resource.label: Greenhouse Job Board API - unauthenticated JSON endpoints for a company's live requisitions (diff weekly for new postings)

subtopics.name: Per-application tailoring inside a hard twenty-minute box
subtopics.learn: Three artifacts, one timebox, no exceptions. Resume: maintain two or three master variants (data and infrastructure heavy, AI-application heavy, customer-facing delivery heavy) and pick one - change only the summary line and the bullet ordering, never rewrite per company, because per-company rewriting is where searches die at eight applications a month. Proof link: point at the single case study whose framing matches the requisition's top stated requirement, not at your whole portfolio. Note: exactly three sentences - their requirement in their words, the artifact that proves it, and one line about their product that could not be pasted into another company's application. Twenty minutes end to end; if you cannot hit that, the artifacts are wrong rather than the process.

resource.label: GitHub Docs - Writing on GitHub (READMEs, links, formatting for proof artifacts)

subtopics.name: Backward-planning the convergence so offers land in one two-week window
subtopics.learn: Pick a target decision date D and work backwards with real durations: offer paperwork and team match 5-10 business days, loop start to onsite 3-5 weeks, application to loop start 1-3 weeks. So a slow large-company process you want at offer stage on D must be applied to around D minus 8 weeks, while a fast startup is D minus 4. That asymmetry is the whole reason waves are staggered rather than simultaneous - you deliberately start the slowest loops first and the fastest last so the decisions arrive together. When one company runs ahead, do not stall it; stalling reads as disinterest and recruiters notice. Accelerate the others instead, with the honest line 'I have a process concluding on the 14th and would love to have your decision by then - what can I do to help you get there', which routinely moves final rounds forward by one to two weeks.

resource.label: GAO Schedule Assessment Guide (GAO-16-89G) - critical path, activity durations, backward planning and schedule acceleration

subtopics.name: Scheduling mechanics, timezone discipline and the energy budget
subtopics.learn: Parallel loops fail on logistics far more often than on ability, so make the rules hard: at most one loop-stage interview per day and three per week, never two full onsites in the same week, a 90-minute prep block scheduled before every technical round and a 20-minute write-up immediately after while it is fresh (that write-up is the input to your postmortems). Publish two fixed interview windows per day to recruiters rather than opening your whole calendar, and use a scheduling link only when they ask for one. Always confirm times in the other party's timezone in writing and put the IANA zone in the invite - a US-Pacific loop coordinated from IST across a daylight-saving boundary is exactly where a missed round happens. Thirty-minute buffer after every interview, no exceptions.

resource.label: Google Calendar API - events, time zones and scheduling

subtopics.name: Recruiter comms protocol: the six messages you will send forty times
subtopics.learn: Write them once, personalise only the first sentence. (1) Referral follow-up to the recruiter naming the referrer. (2) Screen prep reply confirming logistics and asking two real questions about the team's deployment work. (3) Day-7 status nudge that carries new information so there is a reason to reply. (4) The compensation deflection: 'I'd rather understand the role and level first - I'm sure you have a band for this level, what is it?' and, if pressed a second time, a range anchored on published market data for that level and location with your number at the top of it. Never state a number first, never disclose current compensation, and set comp_anchor_given to TRUE the moment you slip so you can see the damage later. (5) Post-loop note adding one substantive point you would have made with five more minutes. (6) The acceleration email when another process is converging.

resource.label: Patrick McKenzie - Salary Negotiation: Make More Money, Be More Valued (never give a number first, and the exact deflection scripts)

subtopics.name: Offer stage: exploding deadlines, extension asks, running finalists honestly
subtopics.learn: The moment offer one lands, execute in order. Be genuinely enthusiastic and accept or decline nothing on the call. Get everything in writing: base, bonus target, sign-on, equity as a unit count plus strike, vesting schedule, cliff and refresh policy, level, start date and remote or travel policy. Ask for the decision deadline and, if it is under seven days, ask once with a reason - 'I have two processes concluding the week of the 14th, can we make the deadline the 16th?' - which most companies grant, and a company that flatly refuses has told you something useful about how it treats people. Same day, email every other live company with a true statement: you have an offer, here is the date, they are a top choice, can the process be accelerated. Absolute rules: never invent an offer or a number, never negotiate against yourself, and never tell anyone you have an offer before it is in writing.

resource.label: Haseeb Qureshi - Ten Rules for Negotiating a Job Offer

subtopics.name: Offer evaluation: normalising comp, equity mechanics, and a pre-committed matrix
subtopics.learn: Normalise before comparing: base plus expected bonus plus annualised equity valued at both the current preferred or 409A price and a conservative haircut, plus sign-on amortised over two years - then subtract the things that are really compensation, especially travel expectations, which for an FDE role at 30% is a genuine cost. For private equity, know the mechanics that decide whether the number means anything: ISO versus NSO versus double-trigger RSU, strike against current 409A, the standard 90-day post-termination exercise window and whether the company extends it, the liquidation preference stack sitting above common, and expected dilution across future rounds. Then score against a weighted matrix over six to eight criteria you committed to in writing BEFORE any offer arrived - learning rate, customer exposure, manager, product conviction, comp, travel, remote policy, runway - so the shiniest offer cannot quietly rewrite your priorities.

resource.label: The Open Guide to Equity Compensation (jlevy/og-equity-compensation)

subtopics.name: The Friday review and the blameless rejection postmortem
subtopics.learn: Thirty minutes, same slot every week, five steps in order: recompute the six ratios and the stage histogram from the snapshot tab; send a nudge for every row where owner is them and last_contact_at is over seven days; clear or kill every overdue next_action; size the next wave from the funnel math rather than enthusiasm; and write a postmortem for every loss. The postmortem is structured and blameless - stage, reason_code from the controlled vocabulary, the single moment it turned, and the one drill you will run before the next loop of that type. Expect 30-40% to land in reason_code unknown and accept that; what is not acceptable is a rejection with no row updated. After three waves the histogram of reason codes tells you what to study, which is a far better signal than any generic prep list.

resource.label: Google SRE Book - Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure

outcomes: You can state your six funnel conversion rates from your own tracker, broken out by channel and by wave, and back-solve the size of the next wave from a target of two offers in one two-week window.
You can show a tracker in which every open row has an owner, a next action and a due date, and no row has gone untouched for more than seven days across a full four-week stretch.
You can sustain three to four loops simultaneously for a month without missing or double-booking a round, with a scheduled prep block before and a written debrief after every technical interview.
You can send a referral request a busy contact can act on in under sixty seconds, and report your referral acceptance rate across at least fifteen asks.
You can deflect the compensation question twice in a recruiter screen without giving a number, then produce the published band for that level and location on request.

You can, on the day a first offer lands, get it in writing with all eight terms, ask for a deadline extension with a reason, and send acceleration emails to every other live company before end of day.
You can compare two offers on a normalised total-compensation basis including equity mechanics, score them on a matrix you committed to before either arrived, and defend the choice in five sentences.
You can produce a postmortem for every rejection with a controlled reason code and a linked remediation drill, and name the two codes that dominate your losses.
failureModes: You apply to your three dream companies in week one, get rejected on a rusty systems round, and burn requisitions carrying a 6-12 month cooldown - so the only companies you actually wanted are closed exactly when you finally get sharp.
You answer the recruiter's compensation question with a number in the first ten minutes, and every subsequent conversation negotiates down from an anchor you set 25% below the published band.
Wave one lands four onsites in the same week; by Thursday you are on four hours of sleep and you fail the one loop that mattered for reasons that have nothing to do with your ability.

The tracker goes stale in week three, two companies quietly stop replying, and you find out the requisitions closed only when you eventually check - the classic silent failure of an uninstrumented pipeline.
Your offers arrive six weeks apart, so you have no parallelism at all and accept a five-day exploding offer with zero leverage while the two loops you actually wanted are still at round two.

You imply a competing offer that does not exist, the recruiter checks with a counterpart in a small market where everyone knows everyone, and you lose both processes plus the referral network that fed them.

You spend your warm introductions in month six on loops you are not yet ready for, convert none of them, and cannot re-spend that social capital for a year because the same contacts now have a data point on you.
interviewQuestions: You are running three customer deployments at once and all three escalate in the same week. Walk me through how you decide what gets your Tuesday, and what you actually say to the two customers who do not get it.

Design the tracking system a four-person deployment team would use to run forty concurrent accounts through a seven-stage onboarding funnel. What is the schema, what is the weekly ritual, and what alert fires when an account is stuck?

A customer onboarding funnel used to convert 30% of pilots to production and now converts 8%. You have stage-entry timestamps for 200 accounts and nothing else. How do you find out what changed, and what would you need to be sure?
Tell me about a time you forced a decision out of a stakeholder who kept slipping the date. What was the exact sentence you used, and what would you have done if they had said no?

A customer asks for a price before you have scoped the work, and pushes twice. What do you say the first time, what do you say the second time, and what does giving them a number too early cost you later?
Where else are you in process, and when do you need to decide? Give me your literal answer - then tell me why you phrased it that way.
You have a signed offer with a Friday deadline and your first-choice company is two rounds behind. Walk me through what you do in order, and what you say to each side.
proofOfWork: Beyond the weekly-updated tracker, publish a short, fully anonymised search-telemetry report - a repository or single page called pipeline-report containing the data and the code that produced it, with company names replaced by tier and industry so nothing is indiscreet. It ships the raw export (one row per application with wave, tier, channel, stage-entry timestamps, outcome and reason code), a ~100-line Python or Apps Script analysis that computes the six conversion ratios overall and split by channel and wave, median and p90 dwell time per stage, cycle time from application to decision, and a small-multiples chart of stage counts over time built from the weekly snapshots. On top of the numbers, three pieces of writing: a cohort comparison showing what changed between wave one and wave three and which specific intervention moved which ratio (for example referral share rising from 20% to 60% and what it did to response rate versus loop-to-offer rate, which is the honest and slightly deflating finding most people never measure); a reason-code histogram across every rejection with the two dominant codes named and the drills you ran against them; and a one-page convergence timeline showing planned versus actual dates for each loop, annotated with every acceleration email you sent and whether it moved the date. The artifact proves three things at once that are hard to fake - that you instrument a system you own, that you reason about a funnel with real numbers instead of anecdotes, and that you can write about your own failures with reason codes rather than excuses. It is also a legitimate answer to 'tell me about a system you built and measured' in a loop where every other candidate reaches for a work project they cannot show.
